title: The raft again (section 6)
hook: even the teaching is to be let go of, like a raft, and how much more what isn't the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, not seen by marks: wherever there are marks, there is illusion. Your line: beyond the marks. Who did you look one step past? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

Subhuti has a worry, and it's a practical one. He has just heard that a Buddha can't be seen by his marks. Strong medicine. So he asks what anyone who has tried to explain something subtle to a skeptical friend might ask: in some later age, when people hear words like these, will anyone actually trust them? The Buddha says yes, there will be such people. Then he reaches for a picture this path has met before, in the older discourses. A raft, built for a river, and a question about what to do with it once you're across. Today: the raft again.
screen: `WILL ANYONE TRUST THIS?` → `YES, SAYS THE BUDDHA.` → `A RAFT, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the worry answered. The Buddha says that in a later time there will be people who keep the precepts, and when they hear even a single line of this teaching, a clear trust will arise in them. The sutra says their roots of goodness weren't planted with one Buddha only, but with countless Buddhas. Second, how they hold it. These people, the sutra says, don't grab hold of teachings, and they don't grab hold of the denial of teachings either. Neither one becomes a place to stand. That's a narrow path. Clutching the teaching is one ditch. Clutching the idea that nothing matters is the other. Third, the raft. That's why, the Buddha says, his teaching is to be understood as a raft. Even teachings are to be let go of, and how much more what isn't teaching. Fourth, the raft before this one. In the Pali discourses, in a sutta called the Water Snake, the Buddha tells of a man facing a great flood. He gathers grass and sticks and branches, binds them into a raft, and paddles across. On the far shore he wonders whether to hoist the raft onto his head and carry it with him, out of gratitude. No, the Buddha says. Leave it on the bank and go on. The teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. The Diamond Sutra picks up that old raft and pushes it one step further: even the teaching itself, even this sutra. Notice what the picture doesn't say. Nobody throws the raft away in the middle of the river. You need it on the water. The letting go comes when it has done its work.
screen: `WILL ANYONE TRUST THIS?` · `NOT TEACHING, NOT ITS DENIAL.` · `EVEN THE TEACHING IS A RAFT.` · `DON'T CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD.` · then, large: `FOR CROSSING, NOT FOR HOLDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: let go of one teaching. Settle, and breathe. Find one rule you've carried for a long time, something that once got you across a hard stretch. Never ask for help. Always be early. Keep the peace at any price. Hold it for a moment and thank it, the way you might pat a raft that kept you dry. Then ask, without hurrying: am I still on the river, or am I carrying this on my head? You don't have to decide today. Just set it down on the bank for the length of this sit, and breathe beside it. The bell holds the time.
The raft again. The teaching is a raft for crossing; even it is let go of, and how much more what isn't the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: even the raft. Today, catch one rule you follow without thinking, and ask whether it's still getting you across, or just riding on your head. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools use the raft picture to say that the teachings are tools for awakening, to be used fully and not clung to.

match.prompt: the raft, twice: tap the pairs.
pairs: a man crosses a flood on a raft
leave the raft on the bank
even the teaching is let go of

myth: the raft picture appears only in the Diamond Sutra
it's in the Pali Water Snake sutta too, where the man leaves the raft on the far bank.
the raft means you should drop the teaching before you cross
the raft is for crossing. it's let go of once it has done its work.
the sutra says people in a later age will still hear this with trust
even hearing a single line, a clear trust will arise in them.

fork.setup: you built a raft from grass and branches and crossed the flood on it. now you're on the far shore. what do you do with the raft?
options: carry it on your head, out of gratitude.
leave it on the bank and walk on.
break it apart so it can't be used again.
fork.reveal: in the Water Snake sutta, the Buddha says leave it on the bank: the teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. the Diamond Sutra adds: even the teaching.

original.note: Sanskrit: a teaching, and also a thing or phenomenon; the sutra says even dharmas are let go of, like a raft.

trapdoor: what you thought: the raft means religion doesn't matter.
what it means: the teaching is a raft. use it fully on the water; don't carry it on your head once you're across.
what a scholar hears: the Diamond Sutra takes up the raft of the Pali Water Snake sutta and extends it to the teaching itself, steering between clinging to teachings and clinging to their denial.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.
All wording paraphrased (quoted: null). The sutra's 'last five hundred years' is left out under the claims rule; the voice says 'a later time'.
'Roots of goodness planted with countless Buddhas' paraphrases the sutra's statement; the Chinese specifies numbers of Buddhas, deliberately left unspecified here.
Hook says the path 'has met' the raft before, in the older discourses (the title says 'again'); confirm that an earlier day of the Buddhism path taught MN 22's raft.
Alagaddupama Sutta rendered as 'the Water Snake' sutta; Keeper may prefer another English title.
